q: 1. Soil can exist in .............
explain: Depending on conditions, soil can be a three-phase system (solid-water-air), two-phase (dry solid-air, or saturated solid-water), or approach single-phase, so all apply.

q: 2. Which of the following is a glacial soil?
options: Deposited at the bottom of the lakes
explain: Glacial soils are transported and deposited directly by glacier ice, which none of the other options (river, lake, sea) describe.

q: 3. Talus is the soil transported by .............
explain: Talus is scree that accumulates at the base of a slope or cliff due to gravity-driven rockfall.

q: 4. In hydrometer analysis the principle used is .............
explain: Stoke's Law relates the settling velocity of fine particles in suspension to their size, forming the basis of hydrometer analysis.

q: 5. Agent of transportation for alluvial soils is .............
explain: Alluvial soils are transported and deposited by flowing water such as rivers.

q: 6. Soil is considered as .............
explain: Soil is generally treated as a three-phase system consisting of solid particles, water, and air.

q: 7. The drop of the cup for the liquid limit determination is .............
explain: In the Casagrande liquid limit device, the standard drop height of the cup is 10 mm.

q: 8. At liquid limit a soil has .............
options: nothing to do with shear strength
explain: The liquid limit marks the water content at which soil has negligible shear strength, transitioning from plastic to liquid state.

q: 9. When the plastic limit cannot be determined, the soil is reported to be .............
explain: If the soil cannot be rolled into threads to determine plastic limit, it is classified as non-plastic.

q: 10. A soil consisting of approximately equal percentage of sand, silt and clay is referred to as .............
explain: Loam is defined as soil with roughly equal proportions of sand, silt, and clay-sized particles.

q: 11. In the field, sand can be distinguished from silt by .............
explain: The dilatancy test shows a characteristic surface sheen reaction in sand and silty sand, helping distinguish sand from silt in the field.

q: 12. Shaking test is also called as .............
explain: The shaking test and dilatancy test refer to the same field identification procedure.

q: 13. The field, dilatancy test is used to differentiate clay from .............
explain: The dilatancy (shaking) test is primarily used to distinguish clay (no water reaction) from silts (which show a dilatant surface sheen).

q: 14. The specific gravity of a soil is the ratio of the unit weight of the soil solids to that of water at a temperature of .............
explain: Specific gravity of soil solids is conventionally referenced to water at 27°C in Indian standard practice.

q: 15. The principle involved in the relation γsub = γsat − γw is .............
explain: This relation for submerged unit weight is derived from Archimedes' principle of buoyancy.

q: 16. The most commonly used specific gravity of a soil in soil mechanics is .............
explain: Grain (true) specific gravity of the solid particles is the value most commonly used and reported in soil mechanics.

q: 17. Hydrometer is a device which is used to measure .............
explain: A hydrometer measures the specific gravity (relative density) of a liquid or suspension.

q: 18. The range of values printed on a hydrometer are .............
explain: Standard soil hydrometers used in sedimentation analysis are calibrated over roughly 0.995 to 1.040.

q: 19. The basis for all soil classification system is .............
explain: Engineering soil classification systems (like USCS) are built on grain size distribution and plasticity characteristics.

q: 20. The degree of saturation for fully saturated soil is .............
explain: A fully saturated soil has all void spaces filled with water, giving a degree of saturation of 1 (100%).

q: 21. The void ratio for saturated soil is equal to the ......... of water content and specific gravity of solid
explain: For saturated soil, e = wG, i.e. void ratio equals the product of water content and specific gravity.

q: 22. The ratio of the volume of air voids to the volume of voids, is called .............
explain: Air content is defined as the ratio of the volume of air voids to the total volume of voids.

q: 23. The degree of saturation for the moist soil is about .............
explain: Moist (partially saturated) soil typically falls in the 50-75% degree of saturation range.

q: 24. The approximate void ratio in sandy soils is .............
explain: Sandy soils typically have void ratios around 0.6 in their natural, moderately dense state.

q: 25. Which of the following clay mineral gives maximum swelling?
explain: Montmorillonite has an expansive lattice structure, giving it the highest swelling potential among common clay minerals.

q: 26. Gravel and sand is a .............
explain: Gravel and sand are coarse-grained soils that lack cohesion between particles, making them non-cohesive coarse-grained soils.

q: 27. The specific gravity of sandy soils is .............
explain: Sandy (quartz-dominated) soils typically have a specific gravity around 2.65-2.70.

q: 28. The water content of soils can be accurately determined by .............
explain: Oven drying at 105-110°C is the standard reference method for accurate water content determination.

q: 29. The specific gravity of soil solids is determined by .............
explain: The pycnometer (or density bottle) method is the standard laboratory technique for determining specific gravity of soil solids.

q: 30. Stoke's law is used to determine the .............
options: grain size distribution of those soils whose grain size is finer than 0.075 mm
explain: Stoke's Law is applied in sedimentation (hydrometer) analysis to determine the grain size distribution of fine particles finer than 0.075 mm.

q: 31. When the hydrometer analysis is performed, it requires correction for .............
explain: Hydrometer readings must be corrected for temperature, meniscus, and dispersing agent effects — all three corrections apply.

q: 32. According to Stoke's law, the velocity at which grains settle out of suspension, all other factors being equal, is dependent upon .............
explain: Stoke's Law settling velocity depends on grain shape, weight (density), and size together.

q: 33. The smallest sieve size according to Indian standards is .............
explain: The finest standard IS sieve size used in grain size analysis is 0.045 mm.

q: 34. Sieving is not practicable for grain sizes smaller than about .............
explain: Below about 0.075 mm, particles are too fine for mechanical sieving and sedimentation (hydrometer) analysis is used instead.

q: 35. A soil having particles of nearly the same size is known as .............
explain: A uniform soil has particles concentrated in a narrow size range, giving a low uniformity coefficient.

q: 36. A soil having uniformity co-efficient more than 10, is called .............
explain: A high uniformity coefficient (Cu > 10) indicates a wide range of particle sizes, characteristic of a well graded soil.

q: 37. Relationship between void ratio e and porosity n is given by .............
explain: The standard relation is e = n/(1-n), equivalently expressed as e = n(1+e).

q: 38. The property of the soil which permits it to be deformed rapidly without volume change, rupture and elastic rebound is termed as .............
explain: Plasticity is the property that allows soil to be remoulded/deformed without volume change, cracking, or elastic rebound.

q: 39. The liquidity index is given as .............
explain: Liquidity Index (LI) = (natural water content - plastic limit) / plasticity index.

q: 40. When other factors remaining constant, the velocity with which as soil grain settle out of suspension depends upon .............
explain: As per Stoke's Law, settling velocity depends jointly on the grain's shape, size, and weight.

q: 41. Degree of saturation of soil is generally .............
explain: Degree of saturation always ranges from 0% (dry) to 100% (fully saturated).

q: 42. Thixotropy of soils refers to .............
options: gain of strength of soil with passage of time after it has been remoulded
loss of strength of soil with passage of time after it had been remoulded
thickening of soil with particles with water
explain: Thixotropy is the phenomenon of a remoulded soil gradually regaining strength over time without any change in water content.

q: 43. The ratio of the compressive strength of unconfined clay in an undisturbed state to that in a remoulded state is .............
explain: This ratio defines sensitivity, which is always greater than one since remoulding reduces clay strength.

q: 44. A sand has e = 0.8 and another clay has e = 1.2, which is more pervious?
explain: Despite its lower void ratio, sand has far larger particles and pore channels than clay, making it much more permeable overall.

q: 45. The coefficient of permeability is proportional to void ratio as .............
explain: Permeability is commonly related to void ratio through the expression k ∝ e³/(1+e), based on Kozeny-Carman type relations.

q: 46. Which of the following soils has largest permeability?
explain: Gravel has the largest particle size and pore spaces of these soils, giving it the highest permeability.

q: 47. The coefficient grain size of soil (D10) is 0.3 mm, the value of coefficient of permeability as per Hazen is (coefficient of Hazen C = 10) .............
explain: By Hazen's formula, k = C x D10^2 = 10 x (0.3)^2 = 0.9 mm/sec.

q: 48. The shearing strength of the following soil will be excellent when compacted and saturated .............
explain: Well-graded sand (SW) compacts to high density with good interlocking, retaining good shear strength even when saturated.

q: 49. The permeability of the following soil will be almost zero .............
explain: Fine-grained content in silty/clayey sand fills the pore spaces, drastically reducing permeability compared to clean sands.

q: 50. The compressibility of the following soil is somewhat less .............
explain: Among these organic/inorganic clays and silts of varying plasticity, OL (low plasticity organic clay) has comparatively lower compressibility.

q: 51. The workability of the following soil is better .............
explain: Being lower plasticity, OL soil is comparatively easier to work with as a construction material than the higher-plasticity options.

q: 52. Soil in which some of the intermediate size particles are missing is known as .............
explain: A gradation curve missing some intermediate particle sizes (a gap-graded curve) defines a skip graded soil.

q: 53. Soil which contains the particles of different sizes in good proportion is called .............
explain: A well graded soil has a continuous, balanced distribution of particle sizes across a wide range.

q: 54. In the hydrometer analysis, the effective depth will be .............
explain: As per the reference answer key, the effective depth of the hydrometer bulb is taken to increase as the test proceeds.

q: 55. Toughness test is also called as .............
explain: The toughness test, which assesses the firmness of a soil pat at plastic limit, is also known as the rolling test.

q: 56. When compared to deformation of thin soil sample because of consolidation, the deformation of thick soil sample will be .............
explain: Because the thick sample has a longer drainage path, its rate of consolidation is slower, so within a given time it shows less deformation than a thin sample (though its eventual total settlement is larger).

q: 57. The time required for the completion of consolidation for a thin soil sample when compared with that of a thick soil sample will be .............
explain: Per the reference key this is left indeterminate; generally, thinner samples with shorter drainage paths consolidate faster than thicker ones.

q: 58. As the value of drainage path increases the time required for consolidation will .............
explain: Per the reference key this is marked indeterminate; by consolidation theory (Tv = Cv t/d^2), a longer drainage path normally increases the time required.

q: 59. The change in the thickness of a soil sample may be due to .............
options: expulsion of pore water or pore air from the voids
compression of the soil solid particles
compression of water (or) air in the voids of soil
explain: Volume change in soil during consolidation is primarily due to expulsion of pore water/air from the voids, not compression of the solids themselves.

q: 60. Standard proctor test is used for determining .............
explain: The Standard Proctor compaction test determines the optimum moisture content and maximum dry density of a soil.

q: 61. Compaction of soil is aimed at .............
explain: Compaction densifies soil by reducing air voids, which decreases the void ratio and increases dry density.

q: 62. The process of compaction of a soil involves .............
options: expulsion of both pore water and air voids
explain: Compaction (a mechanical process) primarily expels air from the voids; pore water removal instead characterizes consolidation.

q: 63. Compaction of soil .............
explain: Compaction simultaneously increases dry density and decreases porosity as air voids are expelled.

q: 64. The most effective method for compacting sand is by using .............
explain: Cohesionless sands compact best under vibratory compaction, which rearranges grains into a denser packing.

q: 65. The ratio of dry density ............. in the field to the proctor's maximum dry density is called
explain: Relative compaction is defined as the ratio of field dry density to the laboratory (Proctor) maximum dry density, usually expressed as a percentage.
